luiz-inacio-lula-da-silva#text: Lula grew up in great poverty in the northeast of Brazil, worked as a metalworker in São Paulo and at the end of the 1970s led large strikes against the military dictatorship. In 1980 he co-founded the Workers' Party. After several unsuccessful attempts he was elected president in 2002 and governed from 2003 to 2010. With programs such as Bolsa Família, which supports poor families if their children attend school, his government lifted millions of people out of poverty. After a disputed conviction for corruption he was imprisoned in 2018 and 2019; the verdict was annulled, and since 2023 he has again been president.
malala-yousafzai#summary: Survived an assassination attempt by the Taliban in 2012 and in 2014 became the youngest recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize.
malala-yousafzai#text: Malala grew up in the Swat Valley in northwestern Pakistan, where her father ran a school. When the Taliban banned girls from attending school there, at the age of eleven she wrote an online diary for the BBC under a pseudonym. On 9 October 2012 a Taliban fighter shot her in the head on her school bus. She survived after operations in Great Britain and continued her campaign for the right of all children to education worldwide. In 2014, at the age of 17, she received the Nobel Peace Prize together with the Indian children's rights activist Kailash Satyarthi.
jacinda-ardern#summary: Led New Zealand from 2017 to 2023 through the Christchurch attack and the coronavirus pandemic.
jacinda-ardern#text: In 2017, at the age of 37, Ardern became one of the youngest heads of government in the world. In 2018 she gave birth to a daughter while in office, becoming only the second elected head of government after Benazir Bhutto to have a child during her term. After the attack on two mosques in Christchurch in 2019 she demonstratively showed compassion for the Muslim community and quickly pushed through a ban on semi-automatic weapons. During the coronavirus pandemic New Zealand under her leadership closed its borders early and for a long time had comparatively few deaths. In January 2023 she unexpectedly resigned.
greta-thunberg#summary: With her school strike in 2018 she sparked the worldwide youth movement Fridays for Future.
greta-thunberg#text: In August 2018 the then fifteen-year-old schoolgirl sat down in front of the Swedish parliament in Stockholm with a sign reading School strike for the climate. Her protest spread via social media, and under the name Fridays for Future millions of young people took to the streets in many countries in 2019. Thunberg spoke before the United Nations, the World Economic Forum and parliaments and demanded that the warnings of climate science be taken seriously. In order not to fly, she crossed the Atlantic on a sailing boat in 2019. Her appearances were widely admired but also fiercely attacked.
wolodymyr-selenskyj#summary: An actor who became president of Ukraine in 2019, he leads the country in its defense against the Russian attack.
wolodymyr-selenskyj#text: Zelensky grew up in Russian-speaking Kryvyi Rih, studied law and became known as a comedian and television producer. In the television series Servant of the People he played a teacher who unexpectedly becomes president. In 2019 he actually won the presidential election with around 73 percent of the vote and promised to fight corruption and end the war in the Donbas. When Russia attacked Ukraine in February 2022, he stayed in Kyiv and with video messages became the face of Ukrainian resistance. He campaigned worldwide for weapons, money and political support for his country.
hernan-cortes#role: Spanish conquistador, conqueror of the Aztec Empire
hernan-cortes#summary: The conquistador who destroyed the Aztec Empire with Indigenous allies and founded New Spain.
hernan-cortes#text: Cortés came from Medellín in Extremadura and went to Hispaniola and Cuba as a young man. In 1519 he set out for Mexico against the will of the governor of Cuba, allied himself with Tlaxcala and other enemies of the Aztecs and marched to Tenochtitlan. After the Spaniards were driven out in 1520, he took the city in 1521 after a long siege. The Crown soon removed him from government but granted him the title of marqués. He died in Spain in 1547.
malinche#role: Interpreter and intermediary for Hernán Cortés
malinche#summary: The Nahua woman who played a key role as interpreter and adviser in the conquest of Mexico.
malinche#text: As a child Malinche was handed over as a slave to Maya on the Gulf coast and therefore spoke Nahuatl and a Maya language. In 1519 she was given to the Spaniards along with other women and interpreted for Cortés, at first together with a Spaniard who had learned Maya and later on her own. She had a son, Martín, with him and later married a Spanish captain. The end of her life is uncertain. In Mexico she was long regarded as a traitor; today many see her as a woman who held her own in a situation of coercion.
moctezuma-ii#summary: The ruler of Tenochtitlan under whom the Aztec Empire reached its greatest extent and encountered the Spaniards.
moctezuma-ii#text: Moctezuma was elected ruler in 1502 and reigned over an empire that drew tribute from numerous subject cities. In November 1519 he received Cortés in Tenochtitlan, but was soon held by the Spaniards in his own palace. When the inhabitants of the city rose against the intruders in 1520, he lost his life. Whether he was killed by the Spaniards or by stones thrown by his own people is disputed to this day.
francisco-pizarro#role: Spanish conquistador, conqueror of the Inca Empire
francisco-pizarro#summary: The conquistador from Trujillo who subjugated the Inca Empire and founded Lima.
francisco-pizarro#text: Pizarro came to the Americas early and in 1513 took part in Balboa's expedition to the Pacific. After two voyages of exploration along the coast of South America, he received the right from the Crown in 1529 to conquer Peru. In 1532 he captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca, had him executed and marched to Cusco. In 1535 he founded Lima as the new capital. In a quarrel over the spoils with his former partner Diego de Almagro, he was murdered by Almagro's supporters in 1541.
atahualpa#role: Last independent ruler of the Inca Empire
atahualpa#summary: The Inca ruler who fell into Spanish captivity after a civil war against his brother.
atahualpa#text: Atahualpa was a son of the Inca Huayna Cápac and after his death fought his half-brother Huáscar for the throne. In 1532 he had just won the civil war when Pizarro captured him at Cajamarca. For his freedom he had a room filled with gold and silver. The Spaniards took the ransom but sentenced him in 1533 and executed him.
bartolome-de-las-casas#role: Dominican friar, bishop and defender of the Indigenous peoples
bartolome-de-las-casas#summary: The former colonist who became the most determined critic of the Spanish conquest.
bartolome-de-las-casas#text: Las Casas came to Hispaniola in 1502 and himself held Indigenous people in an encomienda. In 1514 he gave them up and devoted his life to the fight against their exploitation; later he joined the Dominican order and became Bishop of Chiapas. His reports contributed to the New Laws of 1542, and in his “Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies” he described the violence of the conquerors. He later regretted having at first suggested that Africans should work instead of Indigenous people.
sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz#name: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz#role: Nun, poet and scholar in New Spain
sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz#summary: The most important poet of the colonial Americas and an early advocate of education for women.
sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz#text: Juana Inés de Asbaje secretly learned to read as a child and came to the court of the viceroy in Mexico City as a lady-in-waiting, where she attracted attention through her learning. In order to be able to study, she entered the convent of San Jerónimo in 1669 and built up a large library there. She wrote poems, plays and the philosophical poem “First Dream”. After conflicts with church superiors she gave up her studies and died in 1695 while nursing sick fellow nuns during an epidemic.
zumbi-dos-palmares#role: Leader of the quilombo of Palmares
zumbi-dos-palmares#summary: The last leader of Palmares and today a symbol of the resistance of the Afro-Brazilian population.
zumbi-dos-palmares#text: Zumbi was born in Palmares and, according to tradition, had been carried off as a child by Portuguese soldiers and raised by a priest before he returned to the quilombo. He rejected the peace treaty of 1678 and took over the leadership of Palmares. After the main settlement was captured in 1694 he continued the fight, but was betrayed and killed on 20 November 1695. The day of his death is observed in Brazil as the Day of Black Consciousness.
tupac-amaru-ii#role: Indigenous cacique and leader of the uprising of 1780
tupac-amaru-ii#summary: The cacique who invoked the Incas and led the largest uprising against Spanish rule in the Andes.
tupac-amaru-ii#text: José Gabriel Condorcanqui was the cacique of several villages south of Cusco and ran a mule transport business that made him familiar with the grievances of the population. He tried in vain through the courts to reduce the burdens of the mita. In 1780 he began an uprising and named himself after the last Inca of Vilcabamba. After his capture he was executed in Cusco on 18 May 1781. In Peru he is regarded as a forerunner of independence and a symbol of Indigenous resistance.
micaela-bastidas#role: Co-leader of the uprising of Túpac Amaru II
micaela-bastidas#summary: The wife of Túpac Amaru II, who organised the troops, supplies and communications of the uprising.
micaela-bastidas#text: Micaela Bastidas married José Gabriel Condorcanqui in 1760 and was his closest adviser. During the uprising she ran the headquarters, recruited fighters, provided weapons and food and urged her husband to advance quickly on Cusco. In April 1781 she was captured together with him. On 18 May 1781 she was executed in Cusco before his eyes. Peru today honours her as a heroine of independence.
jose-de-san-martin#role: General and liberator of Argentina, Chile and Peru
jose-de-san-martin#summary: The Argentine general who crossed the Andes and freed Chile and Peru from Spanish rule.
jose-de-san-martin#text: San Martín was born in Yapeyú on the Uruguay River, grew up in Spain and fought in the Spanish army against Napoleon. In 1812 he returned to Buenos Aires and raised the Army of the Andes in Mendoza, with which he liberated Chile in 1817. In 1821 he proclaimed the independence of Peru in Lima and became its Protector. After a meeting with Bolívar in Guayaquil in 1822 he withdrew and left the completion of the struggle to him. He died in exile in France in 1850.
pedro-i-von-brasilien#summary: The Portuguese prince who declared Brazil independent in 1822 and became its first emperor.
pedro-i-von-brasilien#text: Pedro came to Brazil as a child with the Portuguese court in 1808. When his father returned to Portugal in 1821, he stayed behind as regent and declared independence in 1822. In 1824 he gave the empire a constitution that secured far-reaching rights for him as emperor. Growing discontent forced him to abdicate in 1831 in favour of his five-year-old son Pedro II. In Portugal he then fought successfully for his daughter's throne and died near Lisbon in 1834.
benito-juarez#role: President of Mexico and leader of the Liberals
benito-juarez#summary: The Zapotec lawyer who as president pushed through the Reform and defended Mexico against the French intervention.
benito-juarez#text: Juárez grew up as an orphan in a Zapotec village in Oaxaca and only learned Spanish at the age of twelve. He studied law, became governor of Oaxaca and was one of the authors of the Reform Laws. From 1858 he led the Liberals as president through the Reform War and the struggle against Emperor Maximilian. After the victory of the republic in 1867 he governed until his death in 1872. He is regarded as one of Mexico's most important statesmen.
isabel-von-brasilien#role: Crown princess and regent of the Empire of Brazil
isabel-von-brasilien#summary: The daughter of Emperor Pedro II who, as regent, signed the law abolishing slavery in 1888.
isabel-von-brasilien#text: Isabel was the heir to the throne of her father Pedro II and stood in for him three times as regent during his travels. In 1871 she signed the law that declared the children of enslaved mothers free. On 13 May 1888 she put the complete abolition of slavery into force with the Lei Áurea. After the fall of the monarchy in 1889 she went into exile in France with her family, where she died in 1921.
jose-marti#role: Cuban poet, journalist and independence fighter
jose-marti#summary: The poet and organiser of the Cuban struggle for independence who became Cuba's national hero.
jose-marti#text: Martí was born in Havana and, while still a teenager, was sentenced to forced labour for criticising Spanish rule and banished to Spain. He lived in Mexico, Guatemala and for some fifteen years in New York, where he wrote as a journalist for Latin American newspapers. His volumes of poetry such as the “Simple Verses” and his essay “Our America” made him famous. In 1892 he founded the Cuban Revolutionary Party, and he fell in 1895 shortly after the beginning of the war of independence.
osman-i#summary: The Turkish frontier prince in northwestern Anatolia after whom the Ottoman Empire is named.
osman-i#text: Little is known for certain about Osman's origins and youth; later chronicles embellished his life with legends, such as a dream that promised his family world dominion. Around 1300 he led a small principality near Söğüt on the border with Byzantium. In 1302 he defeated a Byzantine army at Bapheus, which brought him a following of warriors. He died around 1324, shortly before or while his son Orhan conquered Bursa. The rulers and their empire were called "Ottomans" after him.
mehmed-ii#role: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, "the Conqueror"
mehmed-ii#summary: The sultan who conquered Constantinople in 1453 and made Istanbul the capital of a world empire.
mehmed-ii#text: Mehmed II reigned briefly from 1444 and then from 1451 to 1481. At the age of 21 he conquered Constantinople in 1453 and received the epithet Fatih, the Conqueror. He settled Muslims, Christians and Jews in the depopulated city, installed a Greek Orthodox patriarch and had the Topkapı Palace built. His campaigns brought Serbia, Bosnia, the Peloponnese, Trebizond and the Crimea under Ottoman rule. He had laws collected, supported scholars and had his portrait painted by the Venetian painter Gentile Bellini.
selim-i#summary: The sultan who in only eight years defeated Persia and conquered Syria, Egypt and the holy places of Islam.
selim-i#text: Selim, later called Yavuz, "the Grim", forced his father Bayezid II to abdicate in 1512 and had his brothers killed. In 1514 he defeated the Persian shah Ismail I at Chaldiran. In 1516 and 1517 he destroyed the Mamluk Sultanate and conquered Syria, Palestine and Egypt. With Mecca and Medina he gained the protectorate over the holy places, which greatly increased the prestige of the sultans in the Islamic world. He died in 1520 and left his son Suleiman an empire almost doubled in size.
mimar-sinan#summary: The most important master builder in Ottoman history, who shaped the architecture of the empire for half a century.
mimar-sinan#text: Sinan came from a Christian family in central Anatolia and entered the sultan's service through the levy of boys. As a Janissary he built bridges and fortifications on campaigns before becoming court architect around 1539. In almost fifty years more than 300 buildings were erected under his direction: mosques, madrasas, baths, bridges and caravanserais. His best-known works are the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul and the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne, which he himself regarded as his masterpiece. He died in Istanbul in 1588.
huerrem-sultan#summary: The former slave from Ruthenia who, as Suleiman's wife, became the most influential woman in the Ottoman Empire.
huerrem-sultan#text: Hürrem, known in Europe as Roxelana, came from Ruthenia, then part of Poland, and as a young girl was carried off by Crimean Tatars and sold to the sultan's court. She became Suleiman's favourite and, against all tradition, his freed and lawful wife. She corresponded with the Polish king and endowed a mosque complex in Istanbul and a soup kitchen in Jerusalem. Contemporaries accused her of intrigue in the execution of the heir to the throne Mustafa in 1553, which is disputed among historians. Her son ascended the throne in 1566 as Selim II.
koesem-sultan#summary: The mother of two sultans and grandmother of a third, who determined politics at the Ottoman court for almost three decades.
koesem-sultan#text: Kösem probably came to the harem as a girl of Greek origin and became the favourite consort of Sultan Ahmed I. After his death in 1617 and the turmoil of the following years, her son Murad IV became sultan in 1623, and Kösem led the regency as valide sultan. After Murad's death she governed again for her son Ibrahim and for her grandson Mehmed IV. She endowed mosques, fountains and caravanserais and supported the poor and widows. In 1651 she was murdered in the palace in a power struggle with the mother of Mehmed IV.
evliya-celebi#summary: The Ottoman world traveller whose ten-volume book of travels portrays life in the empire in the 17th century.
evliya-celebi#text: Evliya Çelebi was born in Istanbul in 1611 as the son of a court goldsmith and was educated in the palace. Instead of pursuing an official career, he travelled for about 40 years, often in the retinue of envoys, governors and armies. He described Anatolia, the Balkans, the Caucasus, Persia, Arabia, Egypt and, in 1665, Vienna as well. His Seyahatname is full of observations on languages, markets, foods and buildings, but also full of exaggerations. He died around 1682, probably in Cairo or Istanbul.
ibrahim-mueteferrika#summary: The scholar from Transylvania who introduced printing in Ottoman Turkish.
ibrahim-mueteferrika#text: İbrahim was born a Christian around 1674 in Kolozsvár in Transylvania, was taken prisoner by the Ottomans at a young age and converted to Islam. At court he served as a translator and diplomat. In 1727 he received permission to print secular books and founded the first press for Ottoman Turkish books in his house in Istanbul. He printed dictionaries, histories and maps and himself wrote a treatise that recommended military reforms on European models. He died in Istanbul in 1745.
selim-iii#role: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire and reformer
selim-iii#summary: The sultan who attempted the first great reform of army and state with the "New Order" and failed.
selim-iii#text: Selim III ascended the throne in 1789, in the middle of the war against Russia and Austria. Convinced that the empire could only survive with modern troops, he created the Nizam-ı Cedid from 1793, an army trained on European lines, and opened permanent embassies in European capitals. He was at the same time a respected composer of Ottoman music and supported poets of the Mevlevi order. In 1807 rebellious Janissaries deposed him, and in 1808 he was murdered in the palace when supporters tried to bring him back to the throne.
mahmud-ii#role: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire and reformer
mahmud-ii#summary: The sultan who dissolved the Janissaries and founded the modern Ottoman state with ministries, a newspaper and dress reform.
mahmud-ii#text: Mahmud II came to the throne in 1808 as the only surviving prince of the dynasty. He had to accept the independence of Greece and came into a dangerous conflict with his governor in Egypt, Mehmed Ali. In 1826 he had the Janissaries crushed and built up a new army. He founded ministries, a medical school and in 1831 the first official newspaper, had a census carried out and replaced the turban of officials with the fez. He died in 1839, shortly before the Edict of Gülhane continued his reforms.
midhat-pascha#role: Grand vizier and father of the Ottoman constitution
midhat-pascha#summary: The reform politician who, as governor and grand vizier, pushed through the first Ottoman constitution.
midhat-pascha#text: Midhat Pasha rose in the administration of the Tanzimat era and made a name for himself as governor on the Danube and in Baghdad, where he founded roads, schools, hospitals and newspapers. In 1876 he was involved in the deposition of Sultan Abdülaziz and became grand vizier. Under his direction the constitution of December 1876 was drawn up. As early as February 1877 Abdülhamid II had him banished. In 1881 he was convicted in a political trial, exiled to the fortress of Taif in Arabia and murdered there in 1884.
abduelhamid-ii#summary: The sultan who shut down parliament and ruled autocratically, sought to rally Muslims behind him as caliph and at the same time modernized the empire technically.
abduelhamid-ii#text: Abdülhamid II reigned from 1876 to 1909. After the defeat by Russia he suspended parliament in 1878 and ruled autocratically from the Yıldız Palace with censorship and informers. He emphasized his role as caliph of all Muslims and had the Hejaz Railway built. At the same time, schools, railways, telegraph lines and, in 1900, the university in Istanbul were expanded under him. In the massacres of Armenians from 1894 to 1896 tens of thousands were killed. After the Young Turk Revolution he was deposed in 1909.
fatma-aliye#summary: One of the first women novelists of Ottoman Turkish literature, who championed the education and rights of Muslim women.
fatma-aliye#text: Fatma Aliye was born in Istanbul in 1862 as the daughter of the scholar and statesman Ahmed Cevdet Pasha and learned French, Arabic and history at home. After a translation from French, in 1892 she published "Muhadarat", one of the first novels by a woman in Ottoman Turkish. In newspaper articles and books she defended the right of Muslim women to education and work and took part in charitable associations. She died in Istanbul in 1936; since 2009 her portrait has appeared on a Turkish banknote.
